back: Changing the genetic material of an organism by removing, changing or inserting individual genes.
DNA made by joining DNA from two different sources, usually different species, e.g. a human gene in a bacterial plasmid.
It cuts DNA at a specific base sequence, often leaving sticky ends.
Short single-stranded lengths of unpaired bases left after cutting; complementary sticky ends pair (A–T, C–G).
notes: Cut the gene and plasmid with the same enzyme so the ends match.

back: It joins pieces of DNA together, e.g. sealing a gene into a plasmid.
A small ring of DNA in a bacterium, separate from its main DNA; used to carry new genes into bacteria.

front: Outline how bacteria are made to produce human insulin.
back: Cut gene and plasmid with the same restriction enzyme → sticky ends pair → DNA ligase joins → recombinant plasmid into bacteria → bacteria multiply in a fermenter and make insulin → extract and purify.

front: Give four examples of genetic modification.
back: Human insulin from bacteria; herbicide-resistant soya and maize; insect-resistant Bt maize and cotton; Golden Rice making beta-carotene.
Higher yields; less insecticide spraying; easier weed control; better nutrition; possible drought or disease tolerance.
Expensive, patented seed bought each season; genes spreading in pollen to wild relatives; pest and weed resistance; reduced biodiversity; health and ethical concerns.
notes: Zimbabwe does not allow GM crops to be grown.

front: Genetic modification compared with selective breeding?
back: GM: chosen genes, even from another species, in one generation. Selective breeding: genes already in the species, over many generations.
